In set theory, a class is a collection of sets, and not all sets are classes.

A set is a collection of unique objects, known as elements or members, that can be anything (numbers, letters, people, etc.). A class, on the other hand, is a collection of sets.

For example, the set of all natural numbers is a set, but it is not a class. The class of all sets of natural numbers is a class.

In general, a set can be thought of as a single, well-defined collection of objects, while a class is a collection of collections of objects.

It's worth noting that the distinction between sets and classes can be a bit subtle, and different mathematicians and philosophers may have different opinions on the matter. However, in general, the distinction is that a set is a single, well-defined collection of objects, while a class is a collection of collections of objects.
